title: Deriving the Fragility Curve of a Single Component
text: Under the lognormal model, a component’s fragility curve is fixed by three numbers: the median capacity \(A_m\), the aleatory uncertainty \(\beta_R\) and the epistemic uncertainty \(\beta_U\). Deriving the curve means estimating these three numbers from the component’s design, response analysis and test data.

title: Deriving the Fragility Curve of a Single Component
text:
Median capacity from safety factors
The median capacity is written as the ground-motion level used in the design or response analysis, \(a_{\mathrm{ref}}\), multiplied by a median safety factor \(F\) (Kennedy and Ravindra 1984).
\[
A_m = F\,a_{\mathrm{ref}},\qquad F = F_C\,F_{RS}
\]
The capacity factor \(F_C\) is the ratio of the component’s median strength to the demand in the design analysis. The response factor \(F_{RS}\) is the ratio of the design response to the median realistic response. Each is a product of sub-factors for strength, inelastic energy absorption, spectral shape, damping, modelling and soil–structure interaction:
\[
F_C = F_S\,F_\mu,\qquad F_{RS} = F_{SA}\,F_\delta\,F_M\,F_{SSI}
\]
crumbs: Deriving the Fragility Curve of a Single Component

title: Deriving the Fragility Curve of a Single Component
text:
Combining the variabilities
Each sub-factor is treated as lognormal with its own \(\beta_{R,i}\) and \(\beta_{U,i}\). A product of independent lognormal variables is lognormal, and the variances of the logarithms add, so
\[
\beta_R = \sqrt{\sum_i \beta_{R,i}^2},\qquad \beta_U = \sqrt{\sum_i \beta_{U,i}^2}
\]

Combining by root-sum-of-squares assumes the sub-factors are independent. Whether each source of variability counts as aleatory or epistemic is decided factor by factor.

title: Aleatory and Epistemic Uncertainty
text:
Seismic PRA separates the spread in component capacity into two kinds.

Aleatory uncertainty \(\beta_R\) is inherent randomness. Even for the same level of shaking, the outcome varies with the frequency content of the ground motion and the response of the structure. More data does not reduce it.
Epistemic uncertainty \(\beta_U\) is lack of knowledge about the median capacity \(A_m\). Further testing and analysis can reduce it.

title: Aleatory and Epistemic Uncertainty
text:
Seismic PRA separates the spread in component capacity into two kinds.

Aleatory uncertainty \(\beta_R\) is inherent randomness. Even for the same level of shaking, the outcome varies with the frequency content of the ground motion and the response of the structure. More data does not reduce it.

title: Aleatory and Epistemic Uncertainty
text:
A family of fragility curves
Treating \(\beta_U\) as uncertainty in the estimated median turns the single fragility curve into a family of curves, one for each confidence level \(Q\).
\[
f_Q(a) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln(a/A_m) + \beta_U\,\Phi^{-1}(Q)}{\beta_R}\right)
\]
The 95% confidence curve is the upper curve: with 95% confidence, the failure probability is no higher than this. The circle in Figure 1 marks the HCLPF point from the previous article.








Figure 1: Family of fragility curves (\(A_m\) = 980 Gal, \(\beta_R\) = 0.30, \(\beta_U\) = 0.35). The dashed lines are the 5% and 95% confidence curves. The circle is the point on the 95% curve where the failure probability is 5% (HCLPF ≈ 336 Gal).

title: Aleatory and Epistemic Uncertainty
text:
Mean fragility
Averaging the family over \(Q\) gives a single mean fragility curve.
\[
\bar f(a) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln(a/A_m)}{\beta_C}\right),\qquad \beta_C = \sqrt{\beta_R^2 + \beta_U^2}
\]
The mean curve is flatter than the median curve, so it gives higher failure probabilities at low accelerations. At \(a = 500\) Gal, for example, the median curve gives 1.2% and the mean curve gives 7.2%.






TipThe split is a modelling choice



Whether a given uncertainty counts as aleatory or epistemic is partly a modelling choice. If \(\beta_C\) stays the same, the mean fragility does not change, but the spread between the confidence curves does.

title: Seismic Hazard and Fragility
text:
The seismic hazard curve \(H(a)\) gives the mean number of times per year that the peak ground acceleration (PGA) at a site exceeds \(a\). Its unit is per year. For example, \(H(a) = 10^{-4}\) /yr means that shaking stronger than \(a\) occurs on average once every 10,000 years.






NoteGal



A unit of acceleration: 1 Gal = 1 cm/s². Gravitational acceleration is about 980 Gal.

title: Seismic Hazard and Fragility
text:
How fragile: the fragility curve
A fragility curve gives the conditional probability that a component fails when it experiences shaking of strength \(a\). If the component capacity \(R\) is lognormally distributed, the curve is (Kennedy and Ravindra 1984)
\[
P_f(a) = \Pr[R \leq a] = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln(a/A_m)}{\beta}\right)
\]
where \(A_m\) is the median capacity, \(\beta\) is the logarithmic standard deviation, and \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. At \(a = A_m\) the failure probability is exactly 0.5.

title: Seismic Hazard and Fragility
text:
Combining the two
Weighting the failure probability at each level of shaking by how often that shaking occurs, and summing, gives the annual failure frequency \(\nu\).
\[
\nu = \int_0^{\infty} P_f(a)\,\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}H(a)}{\mathrm{d}a}\right|\,\mathrm{d}a
\]
A real assessment repeats this calculation for each accident sequence, which describes the combinations of failed components that lead to core damage.

title: Seismic Hazard and Fragility
text:
A measure of margin: HCLPF
The median alone does not show how much margin a component has, so the HCLPF (High Confidence of Low Probability of Failure) capacity is widely used. It is the acceleration at which there is 95% confidence that the failure probability is at most 5%, and it is approximated by the expression below. \(\beta_R\) and \(\beta_U\) are explained in the next article.
\[
a_{\mathrm{HCLPF}} \approx A_m \exp\{-1.645\,(\beta_R + \beta_U)\}
\]
